coherence.reasons: Both run a clean pyramid from governing thought to sections to evidence. X is slightly more consistent in its base case: it uses the pilot's 28% ad cost throughout, and its claim that only Amazon-led can pass all three tests "and build a US business, and only near the pilot's ad cost" is precisely worded. Y's whether / route / how structure maps directly onto the decision question, and its slide 3 ties each condition to slides. But Y headlines Option A's fit on the 25% planning case (peak $1.9M, +$2.4M) and then argues 25% is unlikely to hold. Y also calls A "the only route that fits the board's limits" while its own table shows Japan passing them. These are small tensions on each side that roughly cancel.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred answer: Amazon-led with gates, reject retail-led, reset the $40M ambition, and raise the retail trigger to 20% awareness. Y weighs the trade-offs more fully. It funds in stages with green / amber / red thresholds derived from the model (28% from the payback break-even, 34% from zero 2029 operating profit). It asks the board to pre-agree whether a payback slip to 2031–32 is acceptable, which puts the payback-versus-ambition trade-off in front of the board. It adds a 12-month door test before any national retail roll-out. It also concedes that Japan yields more four-year cash unless US ad cost stays below about 26%, then argues the US case on what it builds. X's gates are more brittle: a 28.6% ceiling with the pilot already at 28%, a volume gate at 96% of plan, and a repeat gate at 31% that the pilot's 29% already fails. X's Japan comparison leans on 2030 operating profit (1.8 times) rather than cumulative cash, where Japan leads. X does keep stricter fidelity to the payback limit and names a stop cost of $2.2–2.4M, which is a point in its favour.

evidence.reasons: Both reproduce the answer key's figures accurately: $10.73 and $4.01 per unit on Amazon, $7.55 on retail, $20.8M peak for B, 4.5% group margin in 2027, and +$2.4M / +$0.4M / −$2.3M at 25% / 28% / 32% ad cost with a 28.6% break-even. Both test the 4.5 units per door and 25% ad-cost assumptions against the benchmarks, reject the $5.2B figure, and treat the 0.71 correlation as not showing cause. X adds two useful points: a 25% duty alone turns the 28% case negative, and a 4% Amazon returns allowance would lower the break-even to 24.6%. Y goes further on the critical evidence. It runs an ad-cost by volume grid and ten cases including a Gaon Lab-style stall. It gives the growth rates the key expects (17.3% against 5.1%). It checks the 300k unit plan against the June run-rate, quantifies FX, and works out what B would need to pay back (a 3.1 times halo or 23.5 units per door). It also states that two of three Amazon-first brands stalled. Each has a minor overstatement: Y says "most" K-beauty is bought on Amazon at a 41% share, and X calls advertising "the one cost Onsoo controls". I found no material numerical errors in either.

revision.reasons: Both keep the CEO's Amazon-first hypothesis with conditions and raise the retail awareness trigger from 15% to 20%, citing the 3.5 median at 10–20% awareness against the 4.0 removal line. That matches the key's expected handling. Y does this explicitly and systematically. It breaks the hypothesis into four conditions with verdicts: US over Japan holds, Amazon over retail holds, the limits hold only if ad cost stays at or below 28.6%, and the 2029 / 15% retail trigger does not hold. It then states a revised answer: retail becomes an option earned through 20% awareness plus a door test, not a dated commitment. X makes the same substantive updates but leaves them implicit inside gate 5, without tracing which parts of the hypothesis survive and why.

overall.reasons: Both are strong, defensible documents with correct core numbers and the right conclusion. Y would serve the board better. It gives a transparent test of the CEO's hypothesis and a wider map of the downside across ad cost, volume, stall, tariff and FX. Its staged funding rests on derived thresholds. It is candid about Japan's four-year cash advantage. It also sets out the specific decisions the board must make, including whether to tolerate a payback slip and how to restate the $40M ambition. X is tighter and more disciplined about the pilot-rate base case and the payback limit, and its Amazon-returns caveat is a useful addition. But its gates are more mechanical and partly already tripped, and its treatment of the trade-offs is thinner.
